courses.subject: CURE
courses.title: Why Culture Matters
courses.description:
This course is an introduction to culture, with an aim to broaden students' understanding of humanities in general as well as the relevance of culture to contemporary society. The course explores the relationships among cultural appreciation, cultural representation, cultural continuity and cultural criticism; it also examines how related knowledge and practices in the humanities are valuable of enriching, on the one hand, students' own value system and lifestyle, and, on the other hand, the overall betterment of society, particularly in the digital age of globalization. The course is not theory-based, but its purpose is to expose the students to the diverse strains of cultural thought and practice that are relevant to contemporary society, particularly that of Hong Kong, China and Asia. Relevant contemporary issues will be drawn extensively to explain the values of the humanities and the need for knowledge of cultural studies in the societies of Hong Kong, China and Asia.

The course covers four sections to explain the breadth of knowledge that can be applied to understand how culture works. The four sections include (1) basic introduction of cultural studies as an interdisciplinary field, (2) media representation in popular culture, (3) memory, history and modernity and (4) community, urban culture and critical pedagogy. The four sections show the trajectory of applying a cultural studies point of view to understand why culture matters in today’s fast changing world. The Chinese and English sections of the course will select from a total of 22 sub-themes to discuss the role of culture to art, technology, education and humanities.
courses.learning_outcomes:
• Students will understand that culture is important in the building of a better society.

• They will also gain the ability in critically analyzing the diversity of values and interests in society.

• Students will be able to draw on a number of disciplinary origins within areas of the arts, humanities, and social sciences to appreciate the richness and the usefulness of interdisciplinary approach.

• Students will gain a critical respect for local histories, traditions, and appreciate the value of culture in humanities.

courses.subject: CURE
courses.title: Introduction to Public Humanities

meetings.location: William M W Mong Eng Bldg 408
William M W Mong Eng Bldg 408
William M W Mong Eng Bldg 402
William M W Mong Eng Bldg 402

courses.description: This course introduces students to the basic concepts and practices of public humanities, an emerging field that examines the influence of the humanities in the public sphere. It guides students through the ways in which humanistic thinking and inquiry can impact community engagement, collective cultural history and memory, policy-making, and the cultivation of empathy. Organized into three sections—Visions, Paths, and Experiments—each part focusing on different dimensions of public humanities, the course begins by exploring the conceptual foundations of public humanism, emphasizing the importance of curiosity, generosity, and collaboration. As the course progresses, students engage with real-world case studies that demonstrate how humanities initiatives can reshape culture and society. Students will also experiment with designing a small-scale collaborative project, which allows them to transform their public concerns and humanistic inquiries into concrete outcomes. These projects serve as a starting point for their further development within and beyond the programs of public humanities. The course is designed for students interested in leveraging the humanities to enrich public culture.
courses.learning_outcomes:
* Upon successful completion of this course, students should be able to:*

1. *Analyze and Develop Public Humanities Projects:*

* Evaluate and curate small-scale public humanities projects, understanding their impact on community engagement and public scholarship.*

2. *Communicate Scholarly Research Effectively:*

* Utilize digital platforms to articulate complex ideas in a clear, accessible manner, effectively reaching and engaging diverse audiences.*

3. *Collaborate Effectively in Diverse Teams:*

* Work collaboratively to integrate diverse perspectives, assess team dynamics critically, and manage project challenges efficiently.*

courses.subject: CURE
courses.title: Research Methods in Public Humanities
courses.description:
This course offers an overview of research methods in Public Humanities, and equips students with the essential research skills, cultural sensitivity, and critical perspectives required to navigate this dynamic landscape. Through an immersive exploratory journey on research methods, students will engage in pilot research for a collaborative hands-on project, embodying the driving ethos of this course: engagement, praxis, and reflexivity. In this endeavor, students will explore diverse qualitative and digital research methods for investigating, documenting, and sharing stories, histories, and other forms of cultural mediation for community engagement.
This course is designed to foster an interactive and dialogic learning environment that cultivates peer collaboration and exchanges of insights. Building on the conceptual foundations laid in CURE1004 Introduction to Public Humanities, this course provides students with the practical skillset needed to unlock the transformative and empowering potential of humanities-based research that nurtures and nourishes the community.

courses.subject: CURE
courses.title: Religion and Contemporary Life
courses.description: Despite their long history, the influence of many great religions can still be recognized in our contemporary world. This course is designed to introduce students to this influence of religion in various aspects of our modern life. It will explore a variety of religious themes such as religious myth, symbol and practice, as well as current religious issues in ethics and politics. In order to illustrate the religious presence in our contemporary life, we shall examine these themes by looking at cases of films, activities and practices that can be easily seen in the world today. It is an introductory course and expects no prerequisite knowledge from students.
courses.learning_outcomes:
Knowledge outcomes

1. To become familiar with the basic themes of the field of religious studies

2. To develop an understanding of the key religious issues in the contemporary world

3. To be able to reflect on the relationship between religion and the human condition in the contemporary world

4. To be able to engage in analysis of religious phenomena, taking into account of the key themes and issues involved.

Attitude outcomes

1. To develop a critical yet sympathetic attitude in understanding religious phenomena.

2. To develop a sensitivity to religious dimension of human life.

courses.subject: CURE
courses.title: The Study of Religion
courses.description: This course introduces the various approaches (such as philosophical, sociological, anthropological, psychological) to the study of religion, and attempts to show how, by utilizing the fruits and methods of these approaches, the history of religions can become the discipline which has religion itself as a proper object of study. This course then focuses on the study of the chief elements of religious beliefs and practices. These will include the phenomenon of religious experiences, myths, symbols, rituals, prayer and beliefs.
courses.learning_outcomes:
Knowledge outcomes

1. To become familiar with the basic vocabulary of the field of religious studies

2. To develop an understanding of the theories of religion

3. To develop an understanding of the key issues in the study of religion

4. To be able to reflect on the relationship between religion and the human condition

5. To be able to engage in a critical analysis of religious phenomena by the key approaches, taking into account of the key issues involved.

Attitude outcomes

1. To develop a critical yet sympathetic attitude in understanding religious phenomena.

2. To develop a sensitivity to religious dimension of human life.

courses.subject: CURE
courses.title: Chinese Culture and Its Religion
courses.description:
(UGEA1450 is double-coded with CURE1122.)

The aim of this course is to help students understand the basic religious characteristics of Chinese culture and the relationship between religions and the daily life of Chinese people. It also helps students to appreciate the richness and diversity of the Chinese traditions and acquiring essential preparation for more advanced courses in the area of Chinese culture and religions. The course is divided under the familiar categories of Buddhism, Taoism, Confucianism, and Popular religion. These traditions are, by no means, discrete and mutually exclusive. It will be demonstrated that they overlap and interact with each other through a variety of confluences and conflicts. Students will also be introduced to some primary source of the Chinese traditions including both textual and fieldwork data.
courses.enrollment_requirement: Not for students who have taken UGEC1450 or UGEA1450
courses.learning_outcomes:
(1) understand the basic religious characteristics of Chinese Culture

(2) appreciate the diversity of Chinese Culture

(3) able to have a comprehensive understanding of the essential characteristics of Chinese civilization through a cross-disciplinary approach

(4) learn to appreciate and evaluate, by way of an integrated approach, their own cultural heritage from a broad. historical, social and intellectual perspective.

courses.subject: CURE
courses.title: World Religions

meetings.location: William M W Mong Eng Bldg 713

courses.description:
(UGED1400 is double-coded with CURE1123.)

This course provides an introduction to some major religious traditions in the world from a phenomenological and historical point of view. Topics include Christianity, Judaism, Islam, Hinduism, Buddhism, Confucianism, Daoism and Local religions etc.. Through the study of religion in different cultures, this course seeks to broaden students' horizons and widen their academic experience.
courses.enrollment_requirement: Not for students who have taken UGED1400.
courses.learning_outcomes:
Knowledge Outcomes:

(1) Students will be able to understand world religions in their historical settings and contemporary contexts of modern living; globally, locally and in their many facets

* (2) Students will be able to engage in a* critical analysis of religions by the methods of the humanities and social sciences

Skill Outcomes

(1) Students will be able to develop their skills associated with data gathering and direct observation; organizing it, understanding it, and presenting it.

(2) Students will be able to develop their skills in cross-cultural understanding and intercultural literacy.

Attitude Outcomes

(1) Students will be able to develop their ability to have a critical and yet sympathetic understanding and appreciation of religious traditions especially those one does not belong

(2) Students will be able to develop their sensitivity to ultimate concern and religious dimension of human life

courses.subject: CURE
courses.title: Study of Christianity
courses.description:
(UGED1520 is double-coded with CURE1124.)

The primary aim of this course is to provide students a broad and comprehensive understanding of the Christian faith through introducing its characteristics, traditions, history, scripture, theology and ethics. It helps students to analyse critically the various forms of Christianity and appreciate the richness of the Christian religion that exerts so great influences on human civilizations. Through interdisciplinary dialogues, this course also aims at helping students to see how the Christian faith understands and deals with problems, predicaments, political and ethical dilemmas of humanity.
courses.learning_outcomes:
Knowledge:

* To achieve proper understanding of Christianity as a global phenomenon and some of the representative manifestations of Christianity in various local contexts.
* To obtain a comprehensive knowledge of the major aspects of Christian faith, especially its views of the meaning of human life.
* To have a basic understanding of the methodology involved in the multidisciplinary study of Christianity.

Skills:

* To be able to use the analytical framework and hermeneutical tools for the academic studies of the religious phenomena related to Christianity.
* To be capable of relating what have been leant from this course to some other academic disciplines.
* To have the ability to reflect critically on one’s own cultural and / or religious tradition.

Attitudes:

* To treasure the value of human life and be sensitive to the related ethical responsibilities.
* To appreciate the diversity within particular cultural and / religious tradition.
* To become more respectful to others’ religions, worldviews and values.

courses.subject: CURE
courses.title: Introduction to Cultural Management
courses.description: Cultural management is frequently perceived as a new terrain both for the acknowledgement of the role of culture in driving economic and social development, and for the dissemination of managerial thought to arrange and plan cultural entities, facilities and services. This course first aims to facilitate students’ understanding of the rising discipline of cultural management, which is embedded in the transformative understanding of culture and the on-going global movement that highlights culture-led development. Second, it introduces the managerial approach to cultural assets, initiates students’ understanding of the relationship between arts management and the market system and government policies, and imparts the preliminary knowledge for the management of the arts. Third, it displays a spectrum of major issues in cultural management, such as cultural policy, cultural organizations and institutions, venue management and event programming, heritage, conservation and cultural tourism and cultural creative industries. The breadth of the discipline as indicated allows students’exposure to the basic cultural management concepts and strategies.
courses.learning_outcomes: In terms of knowledge enrichment, students are expected to achieve the understanding of the discipline of cultural management, including its objectives and values, its relationships with the transformative understanding of culture, the on-going global movement that celebrates culture-led development. Other major issues will also be covered. Students are expected to understand preliminarily the operation of art businesses and cultural organizations in connection to market values and government administrative systems. In terms of management training, students will learn practicalities such as cultural managerial principles, planning strategies and basic skills, issues, challenges and limitations specifically for the arts and cultural resources. Discussions are largely based in the local context, supplemented with overseas and Chinese cases, with an awareness of the variances across contexts.

courses.subject: CURE
courses.title: Cultural Policy and Development
courses.description: The course is an introduction to the nature, functions and making of cultural policies. Making references to examples of local and international cultural polices, it studies the relationship between the making of cultural policy and the infrastructure of power, the ideological influences behind the making of cultural policy. It also studies the latest trends in cultural development and its relationship with policy-making, and the impacts on the development of arts and culture, with particular references to the local context. The course also includes a practical aspect of drafting and developing institutional policy as part of the studies in cultural management.
courses.learning_outcomes: Students are expected to learn about how cultural policy is composed, its scope and structure, and the ideological components behind it within the context of the infrastructure of power, and to understand the impact of cultural policy in shaping the development of culture. The course also intends to equip students with the skills of drafting institutional cultural policy, which is essential for the development of a cultural institution.

courses.subject: CURE
courses.title: Introduction to Cultural Studies
courses.description: Through examining texts, artistic forms and discursive practices that reflect and produce different cultures, students will take part in delineating the working definition(s), methodology and critical awareness of the subject. Concepts such as multiculturalism, diaspora, hybridity, globalism/localism, transnationalism will be discussed. Emphasis will be given to Hong Kong culture as a basic reference point in its contact and interaction with other cultures.
courses.learning_outcomes:
1) Knowledge Outcomes
Basic concepts in Cultural Studies
Historical developments of Cultural Studies in England and its expansion since the 1990s
Critical dimensions of the concept of culture and their relevance to everyday life cultural practices, the working of cultural production and consumption

2) Skill Outcomes
Independent academic research on new concepts
Analytical writing on cultural concepts and approaches of cultural criticism
Presenting ideas through reading and cultural analysis

3) Attitude Outcomes
Proactive in learning and research

courses.subject: CURE
courses.title: Introduction to Film and Screen Studies

meetings.location: Lee Shau Kee Archi Bldg G02

courses.description: This course focuses on the language and the basic theories of film/media. From formal, historical and theoretical approaches, students will learn how to analyze and critique the meaning behind the cinematic images; also, will learn to integrate one’s cinematic experience in terms of emotion and reason, and to develop one’s ability in film criticism writing. In the course of teaching, three aspects will be highlighted including the critical, functional and practical ones.
courses.learning_outcomes:
Upon successful completion of this course, students should be able to:

- identify, describe, and analyze the technical aspects of film as art.

- deeply analyze in diverse ways of critical thinking on film/media, such as the views of genre, auteurship, and spectatorship, and grasp the ways to utilize these different analytical frameworks for the writing of film criticism.

courses.subject: CURE
courses.title: Being Human in the Age of AI: An Introduction to Digital Ethics
courses.description:
(UGED2329 is double-coded with CURE2008.)
Artificial intelligence (AI) and data science are reshaping every aspect of contemporary life—from how we work and communicate to how decisions are made about health, education, and governance. This course introduces the ethical, social, and philosophical issues that arise from these technologies. Students will examine topics such as algorithmic bias, data surveillance, automation, misinformation, and AI’s impact on human agency and creativity. Drawing on philosophical frameworks, scientific research, and real-world case studies, the course encourages students to think critically about how technological systems embody values and power structures, and how they can be governed responsibly. The course aims to develop students’ ethical reasoning, cross-disciplinary understanding, and ability to articulate informed positions on emerging technologies. Through a team-based learning approach, students engage in weekly readings, discussions, and collaborative writing exercises that cultivate both independent judgment and cooperative problem-solving. No technical background is required.
courses.learning_outcomes:
* *Students should be able to:**

1. Analyze and Apply Ethical Frameworks: Identify and apply key ethical theories (e.g., virtue ethics, deontology, utilitarianism) to evaluate the design and deployment of AI and data-driven technologies.
2. Evaluate Global Societal Impacts: Critically assess the social and political implications of algorithmic systems—such as bias, surveillance, and data colonialism—integrating diverse global and cross-cultural perspectives.
3. Construct Ethical Arguments: Formulate and defend informed, persuasive positions on the responsible governance and ethical use of emerging technologies in contemporary society.
4. Collaborate and Communicate Effectively: Work productively in teams to synthesize complex ethical ideas and communicate them clearly through collaborative writing and oral presentations.
5. Practice Critical Reflexivity: Reflect on one’s own assumptions, values, and agency as a user, designer, or citizen within an AI-mediated world.

courses.subject: CURE
courses.title: Disability Studies in Public Humanities

meetings.location: William M W Mong Eng Bldg 804
William M W Mong Eng Bldg 804
William M W Mong Eng Bldg 804
William M W Mong Eng Bldg 804

courses.description:
This course aims to build students’ foundational understanding of Disability Studies from the perspective of Public Humanities, and to explore how it transforms critical frameworks within the arts and humanities. It will guide students to analyze representations of disability in artistic and cultural texts, revealing their political, ethical, and aesthetic dimensions, and to consider “bodily difference” as a key category for cultural critique and social justice.
Students will compare theoretical discussions of different disability models within the humanities and social sciences, developing an understanding of the multiple meanings of “disability” as both a cultural and political concept. The course also emphasizes cultivating students’ critical reading and academic writing skills—including art criticism and cultural curation—while fostering inclusive pedagogy and principles of universal design.
Balancing theory and practice, the course covers themes such as disability and design, performance art, technological development, and global biopolitics. It encourages students to reflect on how modern societies define “normalcy,” “ability,” and “humanity.” Ultimately, the course seeks to equip students with a cross-cultural and interdisciplinary vision to understand and promote the public engagement and social transformation of inclusive culture.
courses.learning_outcomes:
* *Upon successful completion of this course, students should be able to:**

1. Demonstrate a foundational understanding of various approaches of Critical Disability Studies, including its key concepts, theoretical frameworks, and its transformative impact on Art and humanities and cultural critique.

2. Analyze Critically evaluate representations of disability in artistic, literary, and cultural texts, uncovering their political, ethical, and aesthetic dimensions.

3. Understanding “disability” as a cultural, political, and interdisciplinary concept.

4. Reflect on and critique societal constructs of normalcy, ability, and humanity, analyzing how these intersect with issues of race, gender, sexuality, and class.

5. Apply critical reading, academic writing, art criticism, and cultural curation skills, while integrating inclusive pedagogical practices and principles from CDS.

6. Engage with cutting edge theories in CDS such as Crip Theory, Biopolitics, and Design Justice to explore the intersections of disability with technology, performance, and global politics.

7. Formulate strategies to foster public engagement and social transformation through inclusive culture and accessibility, balancing theory and practice.

courses.subject: CURE
courses.title: Feminisms: Thoughts and Movements
courses.description:
(UGEC2273 is double-coded with CURE2022.)

A long-lasting struggle of gender equity was triggered by the women’s movements in England and U.S in the end of 19th century. Feminists fight for equality by publications, demonstrations and organizations. In 20th century, the feminist movement matured. Feminists have been more sensitive to the differences among women of different race, class, culture, religion and circumstances and noticed the importance of differences in unity. This course will introduce the strategies and main arguments of various kinds of feminism. Through learning from others’ experience, history and our daily life, we will understand the development of diversity in feminisms. We can have more understanding of feminists fighting for the right of disadvantage groups by self-review and mutual criticism in different times and culture.
courses.learning_outcomes:
1. 解釋女權運動的歷史脈胳

2. 比較女權主義各種流派的生成與時代變遷之關係

3. 分析近代與現今性別權益事件

courses.subject: CURE
courses.title: Hong Kong Cinema
courses.description:
(UGEC2241 is double-coded with CURE2030.)

This course is a survey of Hong Kong cinema, with emphasis on its contemporary development. This course will cover both textual and contextual analyses: we treat Hong Kong cinema as an art form and introduce different ways to appreciate them and criticize them; we also read these films as commercial cultural products to investigate links between movies and society at-large. The course will introduce basic film theories and film languages. It helps students to reflect on their own relationship with these Hong Kong movies they grow up with, as well as help elucidate the complex relationship between Hong Kong cinema and Hong Kong identity.
courses.enrollment_requirement:
CURE2030 is double-coded with UGEC2241.
Not for students who have taken UGEC2241 or 2774.
courses.learning_outcomes: Students are expected to acquire a general understanding of basic film languages, and to develop basic skill in film appreciation and film criticism. After the course students should be able to understand Hong Kong history and Hong Kong society from the perspective of cinema, with critical awareness of related issues pertaining to gender, class, and cultural identity. They are also expected to understand the intimate relationship between film production and film consumption, as well as the differences and connections between art and commerce in the domain of Hong Kong cinema.

courses.subject: CURE
courses.title: Xiqu and Culture

meetings.location: William M W Mong Eng Bldg 706
William M W Mong Eng Bldg 706
William M W Mong Eng Bldg 706

courses.description:
(UGEC2294 is double-coded with CURE2042.)

The course introduces the student a basic knowledge of Xiqu (Chinese Opera), including its artistic features as a performing art, and the characteristics of different kinds of local Xiqu, such as Beijing Opera, Kunqu, Shanghai Opera and Cantonese Opera. Based on the basic knowledge of the art-form, we will discuss the cultural issues reflecting in the plays and performances. Through the textual analysis of scripts and performances, students will be introduced different topics of Xiqu related to cultural studies.
courses.enrollment_requirement:
CURE2042 is double-coded with UGEC2294.
Not for students who have taken UGEA1065 or UGEC2294.
courses.learning_outcomes:
一、學生對戲曲藝術和歷史的基本掌握

二、介紹當代重要戲曲研究成果

三、啟發同學思考戲曲藝術與當代文化的關係

courses.subject: CURE
courses.title: Understanding Comic Arts
courses.description:
(UGED2326 is double-coded with CURE2051.)

Nowadays comic strip has become one of the major forms of visual narratives in our culture. Both comics and film are visual arts originally developed within the period of late 19th century and early 20th century. Although film has long ago established its artistic legitimacy, comic art still struggle for recognition. However, as Will Eisner put it, comic strip is a “Sequential Art” and has its own unique aesthetic nature. This course tries to inquire the governing aesthetic principles of comics and investigate its unique method of expression. We will also try to delineate the special communication mode of comics and its relationship with different aspects of modern society and culture. Students will learn to appreciate comic art from different perspectives, and strengthen analytical skills for visual media.
courses.learning_outcomes:
1. Through the lectures, students will recognize the aesthetic nature of sequential art and locate the humanistic values and meanings of comic arts for modern society and culture.

2. Through tutorial discussions, student will apply the analytical skills and formal methods to interpret comic and visual texts.

3. Through mid-term assignment (research portfolio on the visual representation of comics), student will distinguish, compare, analyze and criticize different visual and multimedia sources.

4. Through final paper, student will prepare and manage to do an academic research on visual representation.

5. Student will aware, judge and appraise the practical values of the analytical skills and historical knowledge provided by this course after they complete the mid-term assignment and final paper.

courses.subject: CURE
courses.title: Foundation of Visual Design
courses.description: This practical class consists of lectures, readings, hands-on visual projects, and workshops, in which two main software will be taught: Adobe Photoshop and Adobe Premiere. Students will examine visual experiences from the perspectives of creators and viewers and will learn how to design images, edit videos, and add primary visual effects for their projects. At the same time, the practical work with these tools will help us better understand how they are used in society - the modes of thinking and inquiry they enable, their strengths and weaknesses.
courses.learning_outcomes:
- This course covers the basics of visual effects and post-production; students can use the tools as a creative medium in the context of contemporary art.

- Apply essential skills and concepts in the development of critical and innovative design outcomes.

- A broad overview of state of the art in new media art, critical design, and media theory.

- Students will gain experiences from technologies and methods related to visual cultures

and aesthetic functions in learning design.

- Develop students’ aesthetic sensitivity and the ability of visual aesthetic judgment. - Enhance students’ portfolio for job seeking.

courses.subject: CURE
courses.title: Myth, Symbol and Ritual
courses.description: This course deals with the inter-relationship of myth, symbol and ritual, which are believed to play important part in human religious configuration. The human meaning of myth, symbol and ritual will be recovered in the context of social, cultural and psychological effects upon their believers. Meanwhile, theories and historical examples will be emphasized.
courses.learning_outcomes:
Knowledge outcomes
Upon successful completion of the course, students should be able to understand:
(1) the role of myth, symbol and ritual in the human religious configuration;
(2) the various theoretical approaches to the study of religions and their social, cultural and psychological effects upon their believers; and
(3) the way religious symbol, myth and ritual interact with society: how they operate within, and are produced by society.

Attitude outcomes
Upon successful completion of the course, students are expected:
(1) to understand how myth, symbol, and ritual operate, consciously or unconsciously, in our daily life;
(2) to develop a critical approach to examine the various components embodied in religious faiths;
(3) to be able to cross disciplinary boundaries with an analytical mind; and
(4) to be able to integrate theory and practice.

courses.subject: CURE
courses.title: Hong Kong Taoism
courses.description: The aim of this course is to explore the historical development of Taoism as a religion in Hong Kong. It will examine the historical link between Hong Kong Taoism and Taoism in traditional China, and will show how the activities of Hong Kong Taoism reflect the local religious characteristics of Hong Kong people.
courses.learning_outcomes:
1、認識香港道教歷史傳統及源流

2、了解香港道教信仰及文化

3、認識道教的節誕和習俗

4、參訪道觀和道教儀式

courses.subject: CURE
courses.title: Religion and Ethics

meetings.location: William M W Mong Eng Bldg 405
William M W Mong Eng Bldg 405
William M W Mong Eng Bldg 405
William M W Mong Eng Bldg 405

courses.description: An examination of the relationship of the Christian and various other world views to ethical issues of contemporary society.

c.    reflect on the relationship between religion and the human condition

courses.subject: CURE
courses.title: Religion and Food

meetings.location: William M W Mong Eng Bldg 404

courses.description: This course explores the intersection of beliefs/worldviews, health, and dietary practices in various religious traditions. Students will examine how different religious beliefs and customs shape the relationship between food and health within these traditions. The course will provide a comprehensive understanding of the impact of religious beliefs on dietary restrictions, rituals, and the overall well-being of individuals practicing these religions.
courses.learning_outcomes:
Upon successful completion of this course, students should be able to:

* Understand the beliefs and customs that influence food choices and restrictions in various religions.
* Understand the cultural and social aspects of food consumption within religious communities.
* Critically analyse the dietary practices of different religious traditions, including Judaism, Islam, Buddhism, Taoism, Christianity, and Hinduism.
* Critically analyse the role of food in expressing faith and spirituality within religious communities.
* Evaluate the impact of religious dietary practices on health and well-being.
* Apply the concept of fasting as a religious practice and its effects on physical and mental health.

courses.subject: CURE
courses.title: Reading Religious Classics

meetings.location: William M W Mong Eng Bldg 713
William M W Mong Eng Bldg 713

courses.description: The classics of different religions offer a wealth of insight and wisdom about nature, reality and life. Reading important religious classics is an essential way to acquire an in-depth understanding of the crucial doctrines and philosophy of a religion. This course gives students a chance to critically read classics, in their original languages or in translation, from one to two of the following religious traditions: Daoism, Buddhism, Christianity, Islam and Hinduism. The texts will be analyzed with a focus on their religious thoughts, and the traditions and skills of interpreting respective classics. Texts selected for reading may include Zhuangzi, The Heart Sutra, The Bible and The Quran, The Bhagavad Gītā, and religiously inspired literary classics such as The Divine Comedy and The Journey to the West. The exact choice of texts will be decided by the teacher who offers the course in a particular year.
courses.learning_outcomes:
At the end of the course, students should:

1. be able to read, understand and analyse samples of religious classics, with an awareness of the underlying cultural, social and historical contexts.

2. have reached a good awareness of the textual study of a specific religious tradition, and be familiar with the main relevant resources.

3. have acquired the basic linguistic and methodological skills to undertake independent research on religious texts, working on primary sources.

4. have improved basic academic skills, including critical reading, research, writing, and discussion skills.

courses.subject: CURE
courses.title: Classical Arabic for Beginners II

meetings.location: William M W Mong Eng Bldg 408

courses.description: The course 'Classical Arabic for Beginners II ' is suitable for students who have studied CURE2151 Arabic for Beginners I or CURE2180 Classical Arabic for Begninners I. This course aims to continue the learning of grammar and syntax that both Classical and Modern Literary Arabic are shared through writing, reading, listening, conversation, and through the study of relevant passages from the Qur'an. The learning of Arabic grammar and sentence structure is also consolidated. By the end of the course, students are expected to have basic proficiency of the Classical Arabic language.

courses.subject: CURE
courses.title: Introduction to Islam
courses.description: This course aims to give students an understanding of Islam as a religion along with an insight into the crucial issues facing Muslims throughout the world today. The course introduces the beginnings of Islam by looking at pre-Islamic Mecca, the life of the prophet Muhammad, and the revelation of the Qur'an. The beliefs and practices of Muslims are explored through an indepth look at the five pillars of Islam. The variety of Islamic beliefs will be discussed in an investigation of Shi'i and Sufi traditions. The course concludes with contemporary issues of Islam in the world, interfaith connections, the place of women in Islam, and the presence of Muslims as political minorities in the West. In addition to this structure, local references to Islam in Hong Kong will be used to give an enhanced local perspective to these topics.
courses.learning_outcomes:
To be able to understand religion in its historical settings and contemporary contexts of modern living; globally and locally and to analyze how contemporary religious expressions shape and are shaped by global and local cultural, social, and political trends.

Ability to have a critical and yet sympathetic understanding and appreciation of religious traditions especially those one does not belong.

courses.subject: CURE
courses.title: Introduction to Heritage Management
courses.description:
Cultural heritage management presents a complex landscape influenced by globalization, urbanization, cultural place-making projects, technological advancements, economic development, and diverse applications in both the preservation of history and the creative industries. As cities expand and integrate globally, the challenge of preserving local cultural identities while balancing heritage conservation with modern urban needs becomes increasingly significant. In recent years, technological innovations and the development of smart cities have enhanced accessibility and supported cultural initiatives, transforming heritage preservation. However, issues of sustainability and resilience in dynamic urban environments worldwide have also emerged as critical topics and debates within cultural heritage management.
This course aims to provide students with an introductory knowledge of cultural heritage management, along with the theoretical frameworks that shape our understanding of cultural heritage. It covers policy at international, national, and local levels, conservation and restoration practices, funding and resource management, and ethical considerations. While highlighting the significance of intangible cultural heritage, this course will also examine the impact of tourism and the vital role of community involvement, intersecting with issues of identity, technology, urban planning, and conflict. By offering a variety of foundational concepts and real-world case studies, students will gain a comprehensive understanding of current practices and challenges in cultural heritage management.
courses.enrollment_requirement: Not for students who have taken CUMT2004, UGED2285.
courses.learning_outcomes:
* Explore key historical and contemporary examples of cultural heritage projects, along with the theoretical frameworks that shape our understanding of cultural heritage.
* Understand cultural heritage policy at international, national, and local levels, with a focus on conservation and restoration practices, funding, and resource management.
* Examine critical issues related to the preservation, interpretation, and dissemination of heritage, including ethical considerations.
* Develop skills to critically analyze intangible heritage, assess the impact of tourism, and understand the vital role of community involvement.
* Reflect on broader issues concerning identity, technology, urban planning, and conflict as they relate to cultural heritage management.
* Cultivate an attitude of innovation and creativity by challenging assumptions within existing methods of preserving, interpreting, and disseminating heritage.

courses.subject: CURE
courses.title: AI in Creative Industries: Applied Creative Technologies
courses.description:
In today's rapidly evolving digital landscape, artificial intelligence (AI) has emerged as a transformative force reshaping creative industries worldwide. From film production studios using AI for visual effects and script development to advertising agencies leveraging generative tools for campaign creation, the integration of AI technologies is fundamentally altering how creative professionals work, collaborate, and innovate. Understanding and harnessing these technological advances becomes crucial for the next generation of creative practitioners entering an AI-driven creative economy.
This course explores the profound impact of artificial intelligence on the creative industries, including film, design, advertising, and music. Students will gain extensive hands-on experience with cutting-edge generative AI tools across multiple creative domains - from text and image generation to AI video synthesis, audio creation, and generative web/app prototyping. By combining theory with extensive practical workshops and industry engagement, students will learn how these technologies are reshaping creative workflows and business models, preparing them to meet the evolving needs of the creative sector in the AI era.
courses.learning_outcomes:
Upon successful completion of this course, students should be able to:

1. #### Explain core concepts of generative AI, including LLMs and diffusion models, in the context of creative industries.
2. #### Analyse and reflect on real-world cases of AI applications in film, design, advertising, and music.
3. #### Apply generative AI tools to create original textual, visual, or audio content relevant to creative projects.
4. #### Prototype a creative solution or digital product that incorporates AI features using accessible, no-code platforms, demonstrating practical application in a creative industry context.
5. #### Demonstrate ethical awareness and responsible use of AI, including transparent citation and acknowledgment of AI-generated content.

courses.subject: CURE
courses.title: Introduction to the Art Market
courses.description:
The artworld is constructed through a network of individuals and institutions, all of which participate in con-tributing to the wider ecosystem of the global network and marketplace for art. The co-generative or mutu-ally constitutive nature between key players and institutions provides the context and rules for evaluating the aesthetic and economic value of art objects. In recent years, the art market has witnessed tremendous growth, and clusters of new galleries, global art fairs and auction houses have sprung up in cities within both developed and emerging economies, forming an ever-expanding network of art transitions, exhibi-tions, and causing an explosion of cultural activities amid various forms of urbanization.

This course aims to provide students with theoretical knowledge and practical skills on how to identify the dynamic roles and activities of key players and institutions in the art market. It begins with an introduction to the history of art market, patronage system and art market logic. The, various practical skills are covered, including art valuation methods, techniques of buying and selling art, and agreements and laws that govern art transactions. In addition to practical skills, this course also encourages students to critically evaluate the complex relationships between the economy, aesthetic values and social behaviors within the global market-place. Special focus will be on emerging technologies and platforms concerning the global online art market.
courses.learning_outcomes:
Upon completing this course, students will be able to:

• Identify the roles and activities of key players and institutions in the art market

• Explain and analyze the history of the art market, patronage system and art market logic

• Develop skills in art valuation, the buying and selling of art, creating agreements and understanding the laws that govern art transactions

• Acquire personal and social competencies in connecting with the art community and pursuing future careers

• Develop skills in critical analysis concerning the complex relationships between the economy, aesthetic values and social behaviors within the global marketplace

• Develop an attitude of innovation and creativity by understudying emerging technologies and plat-forms concerning the global online art market

courses.subject: CURE
courses.title: Visual Arts Management
courses.description: This course leads students to study various modes and philosophies of visual arts management undertaken in different venues. Aesthetics and art criticisms are critical in directing art interpretation and presentation. Contemporary management of visual arts responds predominantly to the worldwide discussions on modernism as well as various post-modernist writings. In addition, it has to operate in accordance with the prescribed state policy. For this bilateral concern of art management, the course comprises two sections. The first section leads students to study the writings on aesthetics by critics from Plato to Foucault, whose arguments are still valid in inspiring many art exhibitions. The second section discusses the practical concerns and techniques in maximizing the social and economic impacts of art exhibitions and relevant events. Both sections discuss case studies taken from different parts of the world.
courses.learning_outcomes: Upon completion of the course, students will be able to describe different categories of visual arts in professional language; to define and explain the key terms in visual art literature; to appreciate and analyze art exhibitions with reference to intellectual debates on aesthetics; to describe and explain the art policies implemented in East Asia and the West; and to develop independent thinking on the operation and promotion of art organizations.

courses.subject: CURE
courses.title: Gender and Sexuality in Cultural Studies
courses.description: What is gender and why does it matter? What are the significances and limitations of gender as an analytic category? How are dominant understandings and practices of gender constructed and contested in different cultural forms and social contexts? This course is divided into three sections. The first section introduces the basic vocabulary of gender studies and how gender intersects with other forms of differences. The second section explores gender through various cultural products and media (e.g. literature, film, video games, theatre, social activism, etc.) The final section examines key debates in relation to gender in specific social contexts. Upon completion of this course, students would understand basic theoretical concepts for gender analysis and key debates on gender as well as gain the ability to think critically about gender.
courses.learning_outcomes:
Learning outcomes

Upon successful completion of this course, students should be able to:

1) understand basic theoretical concepts for gender analysis and debates on gender

2) analyze how gender intersects with other forms of differences

3) use the key concepts and theories to analyze a specific cultural phenomenon from a gendered perspective

4) critically think about gender

courses.subject: CURE
courses.title: Korean Media and Popular Culture
courses.description:
(UGEC3483 is double-coded with CURE3034.)

This course aims to introduce Korean society and culture through Korean Popular Culture in relation to media and cultural studies scholarship and its socio-cultural contexts. In particular, we will examine the meaning of media and culture and its social changes in contemporary Korea through exploring various emerging trends and cultural studies as methodological tool within modern and contemporary Korean issues. Global popularity of Korean popular culture and the transnational Hallyu (Korean Wave) boom continue to percolate beyond Asia and inspire various critical questions regarding trans-nationalism, cultural imperialism and musical authenticity and hybridity. The course readings engage wide range of various issues and arguments of media and cultural studies scholarship as methodological tools; such as cultural representation, meaning of hegemony, cultural industry/economy and globalism of media, post colonialism, audience of mass media and fandom culture, gender and queer issues, and then further focus on the specific context of Korean popular culture including the pivotal notions of colonial modernity, Japanese imperialism, cultural hegemony in colonial Korea, meaning of Americanization, issues of popular memory and decolonization discourses, nationalism and globalization and Korean Wave, body/gender/sexuality / LGBTQ issue in Korean Media and Popular culture, cyber culture and internet memes, transnationalism and diaspora issues and its aftermath. We actively discuss various audio-visual artifacts including Korean news, music video, films, TV dramas, and pop music in each class in order to understand better the texts and contexts within the historical and sociocultural paradigm of recent sociology, media/communication studies scholarship.
courses.learning_outcomes:
1. Torecognize various conceptual ideas and critical thinking on comprehensive Korean media and popular culture and major issues and historical incidents in relation to modernity, coloniality, Americanisation/Americanism, globalization in Korean popular culture.
2. To explain how Korean media and popular culture and its cultural representation and industrial system reflect and resonate with the various socio-economic, political, colonial/postcolonial conditions of globalized Korean popular culture
3. To appropriate glocal and transnational critical perspectives to examine various Korean media and popular culture and its cultural representations that illustrate how these diverse Korean media and popular culture have become articulated in the global context

courses.subject: CURE
courses.title: Contemporary Art and Representation
courses.description: Contemporary art has emerged as a privileged domain for exploring interspecies relations where various contemporary issues intersect. Thus, this course aims to introduce contemporary art and its representational aesthetics to consider various socio-cultural issues regarding art circulation and its interpretation, the connotation of contemporary art in society. The works of various contemporary artists will be presented in the context of focal issues that invoke social practices, conventional modality of contemporary art scene, shifting art interpretation within the norms and values in a society, relational art and public engagement, experimental use of media. In each week we will analyze contemporary art with specific themes, emphasizing the recurrent motifs and issues in contemporary art and its politics of representation, such as situation and activism, space, ruin and urbanity/modernity, trauma and memory in history, animality and non-human subjectivity, post-human and prosthetic body, gender and sexuality, queer art, magic (the material culture of the weird and eerie, ghost and monstrous iconography), cuteness as a concept reflecting from the contemporary popular cultural reference. Close readings in both academic and art critical practices, class discussion and participation will culminate in a final individual research paper interrogating the implications of representational tactics and strategies of a single artist and/or artwork in contemporary art.
courses.learning_outcomes:
Upon successful completion of this course, students should be able to:

1) Become acquainted with various conceptual ideas and critical thinking on contemporary art and its representation in terms of cultural literacy and practice of art analysis, interpretation, and evaluation

2) Develop students’ art practice with theory and critical analysis to form new ways of responding to the contemporary art and to interrogate the meaning of contemporary art in relation to urgent socio-political contexts

3) Introduce various research-driven artists and their urgent relation to socio-political contexts specializing in critical, speculative, and social art practices, moving image, performance, and visual aesthetics

courses.subject: CURE
courses.title: Video Production
courses.description:
This is an advanced course that focuses on practical application in the field of visual imagery. Students are required to have previously taken CURE2066 or possess a solid understanding of visual design principles, as well as basic proficiency in Adobe Photoshop and Adobe Premiere, along with some experience in beginner-level photography.

The course is comprised of lectures, readings, workshops, and practical image projects. Compared to CURE2066, this course delves further into advanced techniques of using Adobe Premiere and combines them with foundational skills in Adobe After Effects to explore the process of creating various visual effects. Building upon the instructional foundation of conventional elements in video production, such as photography, recording, and lighting, this course also covers and practices multiple shooting methods, including mobile photography, sports photography, and drone photography. These various shooting approaches enable students to effectively convey their creative ideas through rich visual forms, helping them explore and develop their own visual expression style while preparing them for future employment opportunities.
courses.learning_outcomes:
- Gain proficiency in various filming techniques and the editing skills required for artistic creation.

- Master the concepts of storytelling and editing in film and video, enabling effective collaboration with teams and production of visual works across various genres.

- Enhance students’ aesthetic understanding of visual culture and acquire extensive practical experience in video production.

- Enhance students' employability skills to meet the requirements of different video making jobs in companies, enterprises, NGOs, and other organizations.

courses.subject: CURE
courses.title: Chinese Literature and the Bible
courses.description: The Union Version of the Bible (1919) constitutes an important factor in shaping modern Chinese literature and the vernacular movement in the early twentieth century. A large number of works of May Fourth writers (such as Lu Xun, Bing Xin and Xu Dishan) are filled with biblical images, themes, allusions and quotations. Meanwhile, many Chinese translations of the Bible are heavily influenced by the Chinese cultural and literary traditions. For instance, Yan Fu’s translation of the Gospel of Mark employs an elegant style of classical Chinese, while Wu Jingxiong’s Psalms adopts the refined forms of Shijing (The Book of Songs) and Chuci (The Songs of Chu). This course aims to examine the intricate interactions between Chinese literature and the Bible, particularly the influences of Chinese literary traditions on the translations of the Bible and the rhetorical influences of the Bible on the emergence of modern Chinese literature, with a view to widening students’ perspectives in the interdisciplinary study of literature and religion.

courses.subject: CURE
courses.title: Buddhism and Contemporary Life
courses.description:
(UGED3322 is double-coded with CURE3145.)

This course studies Buddhism and contemporary life in the context of the new development of Buddhism. It examines how Buddhism is reinvented and reconceptualized to make it meaningful for men and women living in modern complex society of the information age. Based on the recent development of Buddhism in both Asia and in the West, this course discusses how Buddhism responds to contemporary issues facing contemporary men and women. Topics include the Buddhist approach to economic development and human right, pollution and biotechnology, feminism, Buddhist ethics and the issues of abortion, euthanasia and suicide, Buddhism and interfaith dialogue.
courses.enrollment_requirement: Not for students who have taken UGED3322 or UGED2331
courses.learning_outcomes:
uTo encourage students to probe deeper into the ground of existence and develop a wider context of meaning of life through a critical study of the development of Buddhism in modern society.

uTo help student understand how religion can exert positive influences on human life and modern society through the case of Buddhism

courses.subject: CURE
courses.title: Media Arts Management
courses.description: This course introduces a new genre in the art discipline that employs electronic and digital devices as the main medium of communication. The course contains three sessions. The first session explains the birth of this set of contemporary art practices in relation to the Dadaist movement of the early twentieth century that opened up new concepts for visual arts. This will be followed by a session that discusses the range of media now commonly adopted in the discipline, including video, photography, computer graphics, webpage, and the Internet. Different set of techniques are involved in these productions, and they often generate quite different social impacts that affect both the producers and the users. Students are instructed to understand both the technological and social aspects of these areas. The last session comprises a series of workshops that lead students to appreciate and comment on the most featured productions. Emphasis is placed on the angle to promote this new art type as a rising cultural sector in the society.
courses.learning_outcomes: Upon completion of the course, students will be able to describe and define the technical terms employed in the new media productions; to acquire the basic techniques involved in shooting, controlling sound effect, and designing for interactive visual experience; to identify the software and skills essential for creating different virtual experience; to recognize the economic aspects of using multi-media in cultural sectors; to analyze the social coverage and impacts of using the Internet for distribution; and to develop independent thinking about the cyber-culture and artificial identity.

courses.subject: CURE
courses.title: Design Your Exhibition – Curatorial Planning and Practice
courses.description:
“Curator” once referred to an expert in keeping collections and making exhibitions, but has been expanded to encompass a hybrid role in innovation and knowledge creation. Today, curators are active agents in social and cultural transformation, taking part in dynamic projects presented by museums, commercial galleries, non-profit art spaces, biennials, art fairs, and many disruptive platforms beyond the field of art that didn’t previously exist. Curators produce knowledge, engage their audience, spark innovation, and constantly challenge the role of “curator” beyond the confines of the status quo across varied institutional settings.

This course aims to provide students with hands-on experience in exhibition curation and engages students in a broad spectrum of real-world experiences and professional networking opportunities, aiming to prepare students for future curatorial projects/jobs. It covers topics such as idea conceptualization, proposal writing, pitching, budgeting, contracting, publication, exhibition design, installation and exhibition maintenance. By co-curating an exhibition in a non-profit art space in Hong Kong, students will take part in the various stages of exhibition making. With a focus on exhibition experience, audience engagement, and sociability, this course will train students in the role of being a curator and enable students to develop leadership skills and critically apply knowledge conducive to creative outcomes.
courses.enrollment_requirement:
1. Pre-requisite: CUMT2007 Curation in Arts and Culture or CURE2407 Curation in Arts and Culture
2. Not for students who have taken CUMT3005.
courses.learning_outcomes:
Upon completing the course, students will be able to:
• Explain the key roles of being a curator
• Develop skills in the various stages of exhibition making from a broad spectrum of real-world experience and professional networking opportunities
• Acquire personal and social competencies to work cooperatively in a team
• Develop critical analysis skills concerning exhibition experiences, audience engagement and sociability
• Develop an attitude of innovation and creativity by challenging assumptions in the ever-expanding field of curation

courses.subject: CURE
courses.title: Interpretation of Heritage

meetings.location: William M W Mong Eng Bldg 706
William M W Mong Eng Bldg 706
William M W Mong Eng Bldg 706
William M W Mong Eng Bldg 706

courses.description:
Cultural heritage is a dynamic and evolving concept that encompasses various interpretations rather than being a fixed notion. It includes a wide range of perspectives, from Eurocentric to post-colonial, with an increasing focus on living culture that intertwines global and local narratives. This field involves diverse interpretive lenses, public discourse, human rights issues, and a shift from mere observation to immersive experiences. The interpretations of cultural heritage are shaped by numerous stakeholders, including educators, public program participants, researchers, writers, designers, creatives, consultants, curators, scientists, and historians. In recent years, technological advancements have further enhanced the use of digital media and social networking in cultural heritage, fostering new connections between visitors and heritage. Consequently, the interpretation of cultural heritage remains dynamic and fluid, embracing a variety of approaches and philosophies.
This course aims to provide students with a broad knowledge of cultural heritage interpretations and the theoretical frameworks that offer different lenses and approaches for thinking about cultural heritage. It covers various types of cultural heritage, the role of storytelling in heritage interpretation, heritage as public discourse, identity issues, visitor engagement and education, tourism, community involvement, and ethical issues. Additionally, this course will examine how technology plays a role in engaging audiences and facilitating interpretations. By offering students diverse concepts of cultural heritage interpretations, they will gain a comprehensive understanding of current interpretive approaches, emerging trends, and innovations in the interpretation of heritage.
courses.enrollment_requirement: Not for students who have taken CUMT3009 or CUMT4101 or CURE4411.
courses.learning_outcomes:
* Explore key approaches, philosophies, and theories of cultural heritage interpretation.
* Understand cultural heritage as an evolving concept, encompassing various types of heritage, the role of storytelling, public discourse, identity issues, visitor engagement, tourism, community involvement, and ethical considerations.
* Examine critical issues related to current interpretive approaches, emerging trends, and innovations in heritage interpretation.
* Develop skills to critically interpret cultural heritage and its relationship with technology.
* Cultivate an attitude of innovation and creativity by challenging assumptions within existing approaches to cultural heritage interpretation.

courses.subject: CURE
courses.title: Inclusive Theatre and Development of Sustainability in Arts

meetings.location: William M W Mong Eng Bldg 405
William M W Mong Eng Bldg 405
William M W Mong Eng Bldg 405
William M W Mong Eng Bldg 405

courses.description:
The objectives of this course are to deepen students’ understanding of “inclusivity” within the performing arts, addressing the needs and experiences of people with physical and mental disabilities, neurodiverse individuals, older adults, ethnic minorities, people of diverse gender identities and sexual orientations, multilingual groups, low-income backgrounds, and other marginalised communities. Students will master the principles of “sustainable development” as applied to the arts ecosystem, constructing a comprehensive framework that integrates environmental concerns such as green production, social dimensions like equity and accessibility, and economic aspects involving viable operational models. The course will also develop students’ practical creative and production skills by guiding them to design a theatre or arts project that upholds both “accessibility” and “low-carbon/circular” principles, including all practical aspects such as budgeting, venue selection, promotion, risk management, and evaluation. Furthermore, students will establish ethical and collaborative working methods, learning to co-create with communities while avoiding tokenistic representations and exploitative participation, especially within the context of Hong Kong. Finally, students will enhance their abilities in critical evaluation, assessing the effectiveness of inclusivity and sustainability using both qualitative and quantitative approaches, and formulating strategies for ongoing improvement.

The core themes of the course encompass a range of essential concepts. Firstly, “inclusive aesthetics” involves raising accessibility from merely a support measure to a deliberate creative language and aesthetic decision. Secondly, the principle of “accessibility by design” focuses on universal design practices, including relaxed performances, audio description, subtitles or sign language, and ensuring accessible front-of-house and information design. The third theme, “sustainable production”, addresses environmentally responsible approaches such as material recycling, establishing low-carbon stage setups, green procurement processes, waste reduction initiatives, efficient touring logistics, and energy management. The course also explores Hong Kong’s cultural and policy context, considering aspects like funding systems, venue regulations, audience profiles, educational linkages, social welfare partnerships, and community networks. Finally, themes of ethics, power, and representation are central, guiding students through issues of co-authorship, obtaining consent for data and image use, maintaining creative safety, and respecting care and boundaries within collaborative settings.
courses.enrollment_requirement: Pre-requisite: CURE2412 Performing Arts Management or CUMT3002 Performing Arts Management or CURE3408 Curating and Managing Arts Festival or CUMT3008 Curating and Managing Arts Festival
courses.learning_outcomes:
Upon successful completion of this course, students should be able to:

1. Learn to create the inclusion theatre for different purposes, which are the theatre made by the disabled, the theatre for the disabled and the concept of promoting fairness and equality [Introduction to create the inclusion theatre].
2. Learn to create comprehensive accessibility plans for performances, including elements such as subtitling, audio description, sign language interpretation, relaxation sessions, tactile tours, accessible front-of-house routes, and sensitive information alerts. Examine potential barriers throughout the ‘Audience Journey’—from information access and ticketing to arrival, seating, viewing, and departure [Competence (Inclusion)].
3. Implement simplified carbon accounting for stage productions, focusing on four key sources: materials, transport, energy, and waste. Design circular scenography by developing strategies for renting, recycling, repurposing, and modularising sets and costumes [The Idea of Sustainability].
4. Integrate inclusivity and sustainability into an executable team project proposal, covering aspects such as creative concept, target audience, collaboration methods, timeline, budget, staffing, risk management, and evaluation metrics [Implementation Capability].
5. Design foundational assessments using surveys, interviews, observations, and focus groups. Present outcomes and impacts through frameworks such as the Sustainable Development Goals (SDGs) or the theory of change [Research and Evaluation Competence].
6. Facilitate cross-disciplinary collaboration and ensure clear communication with social welfare organisations, arts administrators, front-of-house teams, technical crews, and accessibility consultants [Communication and Collaboration].

courses.subject: CURE
courses.title: Museum Studies

meetings.location: William M W Mong Eng Bldg 706

courses.description:
Museums have multiple roles in a society. They are academic institutes and public arenas for education. In the broad term, they represent national culture and communal heritage. This course leads students to understand museum exhibitions and management within social contexts. The lectures respond to the following issues:
1. What are the functions and achievements of museum activities?
2. In what ways can we understand and learn from an exhibition? What are the essential elements of museum catalogues and cultural writing?
3. How do museum workers balance both marketing and social needs?
4. In what ways can we participate in the operation of a museum?
The course draws discussions from both the perspectives of museum workers and visitors. Some current issues concerning the roles of museums are also covered.
courses.enrollment_requirement: Not for students who have taken CUMT3108 or ANTH4720 or HIST5514

courses.subject: CURE
courses.title: Graduation Thesis
courses.description: This course provides an opportunity for students to undertake supervised study on a selected topic of interest. Students will be led to examine aspects of the selected topic, conduct a critical literature review and a systematic investigation of the topic they have chosen. Students are required to regularly discuss with the teacher concrete findings in their research and submit written progress reports as scheduled by the teacher and a complete project report at the end of the term.
courses.learning_outcomes:
1. Apply theory critically to analyse cultural texts they interested.
2. Use a self-reflective approach to devising and developing an academic paper.
3. Reflectively evaluate their learning and personal planning processes.

courses.subject: CURE
courses.title: Summer Internship
courses.description: Process of cultural production and cultural practices at various levels are essential to the training of cultural sensitivity and analysis in cultural studies. This course aims to provide students with on-site experience of cultural production and practices for their reflection and integration of cultural theories and concepts they learnt in regular classes. Students will be introduced to a range of cultural institutions and culture-related non-governmental organizations for a placement of eight weeks between May to July during summer. Students will be asked to attend several sessions of orientations and evaluation before and during their placement.
courses.learning_outcomes:
Objectives:
Provide learning and practicing opportunities for students

courses.learning_outcomes:
As representatives of the Department, students are expected to behave with dedication professional integrity.

Students will be able to understand how academic training both informs, and is informed by practice.

Students will be able to develop their communication and presentational (oral and written) skills as well as analytical and problem solving ability.

courses.subject: CURE
courses.title: Integrated Studies in Cultural Management
courses.description: This course is continuation of CUMT1001, Introduction to Cultural Management, and looks at cultural management from the macro perspective. Successful culture managers work to maintain healthy balance between culture and its relevant fields of interests, which sometimes could turn harmful or beneficial to the growth and development of the corresponding cultural area. The first session discusses the mutual dependence between culture and various areas, which include laws, economy, community, national interests, and art practitioners. In practice, cultural managers usually have to conform to the values and ethnics of the corresponding countries. For that reason, the second session will look at the approach taken in a few remarkable examples, which Taiwan, China, Singapore, South Korea, U.K., and the U.S.
courses.learning_outcomes: Upon completion of the course, students will be able to explain different national and social concerns for preserving culture; to identify the legal and ethnic issues relevant to cultural productions; to identify marketing strategies in cultural promotion; to evaluate the measures for maximizing the input of art practitioners; and to describe the various successful cultural schemes implemented in overseas countries.

courses.subject: CURE
courses.title: Culture-led City Development
courses.description: This course aims to provide students with a comprehensive understanding of the culture-led city development phenomenon and equip them with the protocols for execution and practice. It comprises three blocks: Block 1 unfolds an overall picture of the phenomenon, introduces the related concepts, displays the disciplinary foundation of this topic, traces its history, and discusses the rationales and developing tendency. Block 2 studies the urban sociological and economic approaches employed in developing the theoretical foundation, highlighting a transition in capitalist production mode and urban governance upheld by public-private partnership modes. Criticisms are also presented to complete a dialectic mindset of this phenomenon. With a strong practical dimension, Block 3 teaches students various methods to make consultancy and policy recommendations for culture-led urban development projects. A variety of practices that constitute the culture-led strategy are discussed, such as how to plan for a creative city and cultural facilities, how to boost creative industries and develop cultural quarters and creative clusters, as well as how to revitalize historic quarters.
courses.learning_outcomes: Students are introduced to the basic concept of the culture-led urban development phenomenon, recognizing related concepts, understanding its history, and developing tendencies in the world. Then, they can gain a deep theoretical understanding of the origins of these practices in a capitalist political economic transition, the corresponding urban policies, and the urban governance modes. Moreover, students can learn how to conduct policy analysis and apply urban planning and design principles to provide consultancy for culture-led city development projects. The final products of group projects shall consist of policy recommendations and project consultancies for the Hong Kong government or other private sector developers.

courses.subject: CURE
courses.title: Special Topic in Creative Industries
courses.description:
In recent years, the rapid development of cultural and creative industries has transformed the way cultural products are created, produced and distributed. These industries, from theater and fashion to social media and game design, highlight how contemporary societies use intellectual and creative approaches to gain economic and symbolic competitiveness. Alongside technological innovations, the creative sector also plays a significant role in driving global economic transformation, offering government agencies and entrepreneurs new strategies to produce creative experiences not anticipated in the past.

This course aims to provide students with both analytical and practical skills in cultural and creative industries. Students will engage with a diverse range of topics, exploring how various sectors within these industries inform a variety of theories and practices. By covering multiple creative and entrepreneurial strategies in the ever-expanding field of cultural and creative industries, this course will equip students with the ability to reflect on the current phenomenon and create projects that have the potential to impact individuals and societies.
courses.learning_outcomes:
* Explain key historical and contemporary examples of creative industries, relating them to a broader local and global context
* Examine critical issues concerning how different cultural and economic models impact the creative industries
* Develop skills to critically analyze the relationship between culture, society and the economy
* Acquire personal and social competencies relating to the creative industries, and act as an active agent in producing creative projects
* Develop an attitude of innovation and creativity by challenging assumptions within the creative industries
